title: How Beautiful the Feet: Your God Reigns
summary: Zion is told to wake, put on her beautiful garments, and shake off the dust and chains of captivity, because the LORD will redeem her without money. A messenger runs across the mountains with good news, the watchmen shout for joy, and the exiles are told to leave Babylon, carrying the temple vessels, with God going before and behind them. The chapter ends by introducing the Servant who will be highly exalted after being disfigured beyond human likeness, the opening of the fourth Servant Song.
story:
The double call “Awake, awake” rang out in 51:9, addressed to the arm of the LORD, and again in 51:17, addressed to Jerusalem drunk with the cup of God's wrath. Here it comes a third time, addressed to Zion herself, and now she is told to dress for a festival. Everything in chapters 40 to 51 has been building toward this: the announcement that God is coming home to Jerusalem and bringing his people with him. Chapter 40 opened with “Comfort, comfort My people” and a herald on a high mountain crying “Here is your God!” (40:1, 40:9). Verses 7 to 12 bring that scene to its high point: the runner arrives, the watchmen see the LORD return, and the ruins sing because he has comforted his people.

Then, with no transition, verse 13 begins the fourth and last Servant Song, which runs to the end of chapter 53. The placement matters. The good news that God reigns and the portrait of a disfigured Servant sit side by side, and the song explains how God's victory will actually be won and how the deeper exile, sin itself, will be ended. What follows in chapters 54 and 55 is the result: a barren city told to sing, an everlasting covenant, and an open invitation to everyone who is thirsty.
historical:
Verses 3 to 5 compress Israel's history of oppression into three stages. Jacob's family went down to Egypt as guests and became slaves. Assyria destroyed the northern kingdom in 722 BC and devastated Judah in 701 BC. Now a third power, unnamed in the chapter but clearly Babylon, holds the people captive; Nebuchadnezzar had deported Judeans in 597 and 586 BC and burned the temple. Cuneiform tablets published in 2014 by Laurie Pearce and Cornelia Wunsch, many from a Babylonian settlement called Al-Yahudu, ‘Judahtown’, and dated from 572 BC onward, show Judean exiles living as tenant farmers on crown land and paying rents and service, and they record Hebrew names built on the divine name. These were the people to whom the prophet says ‘go out from there’ (verse 11).

The command to leave fits the moment after Cyrus of Persia took Babylon. The Babylonian chronicle of Nabonidus records that Cyrus's army entered Babylon without a battle in October 539 BC and that Cyrus himself entered a few weeks later. The Cyrus Cylinder, a clay foundation text found at Babylon by Hormuzd Rassam in 1879 and now in the British Museum, has Cyrus claim that he returned the images of gods to their sanctuaries and gathered their former inhabitants and returned them to their homes. It does not mention Judah, but it shows the policy that Ezra 1:1-4 and 6:3-5 describe for Jerusalem. Ezra 1:7-11 records that Cyrus gave back the gold and silver vessels Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the temple (2 Kings 25:13-15), and that Sheshbazzar, the prince of Judah, brought 5,400 of them up from Babylon to Jerusalem. The instruction in verse 11 that those who carry the vessels of the LORD must purify themselves fits that event closely, whether it is read as address to the exiles of the 530s or as prophecy of it from an earlier century (see the hard question below).

The returning community was small and poor, and Jerusalem's walls were not rebuilt until Nehemiah's governorship, about 445 BC. The grand language of verses 1 to 12, a city never again entered by the uncircumcised and a return witnessed by all the ends of the earth, was not exhausted by that first return, which is why later Jewish and Christian readers heard the chapter as a promise still reaching forward.
cultural:
News in the ancient world traveled on foot. A runner coming over the hills toward a city could be seen by the watchmen on its walls long before he arrived, and they tried to read his news from his pace and bearing. In 2 Samuel 18:24-27 David's watchman, on the roof of the gate at Mahanaim, sees two runners approaching and identifies the first by the way he runs before anyone knows what he carries. The verb for bringing news (basar) is used there and in 1 Samuel 31:9 for reports of a battle's outcome. Nahum 1:15 uses almost the same words as verse 7 for a herald on the mountains announcing the fall of Nineveh. The messenger of verse 7 brings the best possible news: peace, good, salvation, and the words “Your God reigns.” To a people whose God had seemed defeated by Babylon's gods, this was the announcement that he was king after all. The phrase echoes the cry of the enthronement psalms, “The LORD reigns” (Psalm 93:1, 96:10, 97:1, 99:1), sung in the temple before the exile.

The language of verses 3 to 5 comes from the slave market and family law. In Israel a go'el, a kinsman-redeemer, was the relative obliged to buy back a family member sold into debt slavery or land that had been sold (Leviticus 25:25, 47-49), as Boaz did for Naomi's family in Ruth 4. God speaks as Israel's go'el. Because he never received a price when he handed his people over (the book of Judges speaks of him selling them into their enemies' hands, Judges 2:14, 4:2), he owes no price to recover them. Ancient conquerors also claimed that their victories proved their gods stronger; Assyrian and Babylonian kings carried off the images of defeated peoples' gods. That is why verse 5 says God's name is despised all day long: Judah's defeat looked like the LORD's defeat.

The instructions for departure recall the exodus while changing it. At the first Passover Israel ate in haste, dressed to flee Egypt (Exodus 12:11, Deuteronomy 16:3). This time they will not leave in a hurry, because the LORD goes before them and guards the rear, as the pillar of cloud moved from the front of Israel's column to its rear at the Red Sea (Exodus 14:19-20). The rear guard (measef) was the unit that gathered stragglers at the back of the march, the position held by Dan's tribe in the wilderness (Numbers 10:25). The call to touch nothing unclean reflects the holiness required of the Levites who carried the sacred vessels (Numbers 4:15). Garments of splendor (verse 1) suggest festival or bridal clothing, the opposite of the sackcloth and dust of mourning; sitting in the dust was the posture of a mourner or a captive, and the command to rise and sit enthroned reverses the fate of Babylon, ordered down into the dust in 47:1.
literary:
The chapter has three movements. Verses 1 to 6 are God's call to Zion and an explanation of why he must act. The call is the third of a series of doubled imperatives (51:9, 51:17, 52:1), and a fourth, “Depart, depart” (verse 11), will close the scene; the doubling gives the whole section the urgency of an alarm. Verses 3 to 6 are prose-like speech, each introduced by a messenger formula (“this is what the LORD says”, “declares the LORD”), and they turn on the word ‘for nothing’ (chinnam in verse 3, efes in verse 4, chinnam again in verse 5). Verses 7 to 12 are a scene painted in quick strokes: the runner's feet on the mountains, the watchmen's voices, the ruins breaking into song, the LORD's bared arm before the nations, and the procession out of Babylon. The herald's message climbs from peace to good to salvation to its summit, “Your God reigns.” Verse 10 is nearly identical to Psalm 98:3, so the prophet sets the return to the music of the temple's hymns.

Verses 13 to 15 begin the fourth Servant Song, which scholars since Bernhard Duhm's commentary of 1892 have treated as a unit running from 52:13 to 53:12; Duhm identified the four songs as 42:1-4 (or 1-7), 49:1-6, 50:4-9, and 52:13-53:12. The chapter break before 53:1 comes from the medieval division of the Bible into chapters and separates the song's first stanza from the rest. The song opens and closes with God speaking about his Servant (“My Servant” in 52:13 and 53:11), and its first stanza states the whole paradox in advance: the Servant will prosper and be raised high, using the very words of Isaiah's vision of God ‘high and lifted up’ (6:1, 57:15); many were appalled at his disfigurement; and he will affect many nations, while kings fall silent before something they have never been told. Verses 14 and 15 are built as a comparison (‘just as ... so’), with a parenthesis in the middle describing the ruined appearance. The link between the herald's news and the Servant is deliberate: the arm of the LORD bared in verse 10 is the arm revealed in the Servant in 53:1.

outline.t: Zion, wake and put on your beautiful garments
Sold for nothing, redeemed without money
The messenger on the mountains: your God reigns
Depart, depart: the LORD goes before and behind
The fourth Servant Song begins: exalted and disfigured

doctrines.note: “Your God reigns” (verse 7) is the heart of the good news here. The return from exile is not only relief for Israel but a public demonstration that the LORD is king over the nations, before the eyes of all the ends of the earth. Jesus began his preaching with the same announcement that God's kingdom had come near (Mark 1:14-15).

God acts as Israel's kinsman-redeemer, buying back his own without money (verse 3), and his salvation is done in public, before all the nations (verse 10). That no silver changes hands does not mean redemption costs nothing: the chapter moves straight into the Servant who suffers, and 1 Peter 1:18-19 says believers were redeemed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ.

Jerusalem is called the holy city, into which nothing unclean will enter again (verse 1), and those who carry the LORD's vessels must purify themselves (verse 11). The redeemed people are called out of Babylon's world, not only its territory, to belong to a holy God; Paul applies the call to the church in 2 Corinthians 6:17.

What God does for Jerusalem is meant to be seen by the ends of the earth (verse 10), and the Servant will affect many nations and silence kings (verse 15). Paul made verse 15 his missionary principle, to preach where Christ had not been named (Romans 15:20-21), and verse 7 his description of those sent to preach (Romans 10:15).

The Servant's story is told from its ending: he will prosper and be raised, lifted up, and highly exalted (verse 13), in the vocabulary of God's own majesty. The New Testament reads the resurrection and ascension of Jesus as that verdict (Acts 3:13, Philippians 2:9).

words.note: Basar, to bring news, especially good news, twenty-four times in the Old Testament, seven of them in Isaiah (40:9, 41:27, 52:7, 60:6, 61:1). The Piel participle mevasser, the one bringing news, is used of runners from battle (2 Samuel 18:19-31) and of the herald of Nineveh's fall (Nahum 1:15). When Jewish translators rendered the Hebrew Bible into Greek (the Septuagint, in the last centuries BC), they used euangelizomai, from which the New Testament's words for preaching the gospel come. Isaiah's herald shapes what gospel means in the New Testament: not advice or a program but the announcement that God reigns.

Gaal, to redeem or act as kinsman, about 104 times, twenty-four of them in Isaiah, twenty-two in Leviticus, and twenty-one in Ruth. The go'el was the relative who bought back family land or a family member sold into slavery, avenged a killing, or married a childless widow to keep a family's name alive. Isaiah 40 to 55 calls the LORD Israel's Redeemer more than any other part of the Bible (41:14, 43:14, 44:6, 47:4, 48:17, 49:7, 54:5). In verse 3 the redemption is ‘without money’, and in verse 9 the LORD ‘has redeemed Jerusalem’: God acts as the family member of a people who had no one else.

Malakh, to be king or reign, about 350 times, most often in the narratives of Kings and Chronicles for a king's accession. In verse 7 the form malakh Elohayikh, ‘your God reigns’ or ‘your God has become king’, echoes the cry of the enthronement psalms, YHWH malakh, ‘the LORD reigns’ (Psalm 93:1, 96:10, 97:1, 99:1). Scholars debate whether the perfect should be heard as a timeless statement (he reigns) or as an event (he has taken up his reign); in this chapter the herald announces that God's kingship, which seemed eclipsed by Babylon, is now being shown in action.

Chinnam, for nothing, without cause, or in vain, an adverb found about thirty-two times. Satan asks whether Job fears God ‘for nothing’ (Job 1:9), and the psalmists complain of enemies who hate them ‘without cause’ (Psalm 35:19, 69:4), a line Jesus applies to himself in John 15:25. In verses 3 and 5 it frames God's argument: his people were sold for nothing and taken for nothing, so their captors have no claim on them, and God will redeem them without paying anyone.

Eved, servant or slave, about 800 times. It can describe a slave, a royal official, a worshiper, or a person chosen for God's work, such as Moses (Numbers 12:7) and David (2 Samuel 7:5). In Isaiah 40 to 55 the servant is first Israel, chosen and upheld (41:8-9, 44:1-2), and then an individual with a mission to Israel and the nations (49:5-6) who suffers and is vindicated (50:4-9, 52:13 to 53:12). The Septuagint rendered it pais, which can mean both servant and child, the title Acts uses of Jesus (Acts 3:13, 3:26, 4:27, 4:30).

Sakal, to act wisely, have insight, and so to succeed, about sixty times. Joshua is told that keeping the law will make him prosper (Joshua 1:8), David succeeds in all his ways (1 Samuel 18:14), and Jeremiah 23:5 promises a righteous Branch who will reign wisely. The BSB's “My Servant will prosper” (verse 13) and other versions' ‘act wisely’ each catch half of the word: the Servant's path will prove to have been the wise one, however it looked at the time. Daniel 12:3 calls the faithful teachers maskilim, the wise, using the same root, an early echo of this song.

Nazah, to spatter or sprinkle, about twenty-four times, fifteen of them in Leviticus, for priests sprinkling blood, water, or oil in rites of cleansing and atonement (Leviticus 4:6, 14:7, 16:14; Numbers 19:18-19). If verse 15 uses this verb, the Servant does for many nations what a priest did for Israel, and the song anticipates the guilt offering of 53:10. The grammar is unusual, however, because elsewhere the liquid is the object and the person is sprinkled ‘on’, and the Septuagint reads ‘many nations will marvel at him’. Many scholars therefore derive the word from a different root, known from Arabic, meaning to leap, and translate ‘startle’. English Bibles divide on the question (see the note on the text).

christ:
The New Testament's word for the gospel comes from the language of the herald in verse 7, and its first preachers read their message as this announcement. Mark summarizes Jesus' preaching as the good news of God: the time is fulfilled and “the kingdom of God is near” (Mark 1:14-15). In the synagogue at Nazareth Jesus reads from Isaiah 61, where the anointed one is sent to bring good news, the same verb as here (Luke 4:18). Peter tells Cornelius that God sent his message to Israel, preaching peace through Jesus Christ (Acts 10:36), echoing the herald who proclaims peace. Paul quotes verse 7 in Romans 10:15, “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!”, to describe apostles sent to preach Christ, and in the very next verse quotes Isaiah 53:1, tying the herald's news to the report about the Servant. Ephesians speaks of feet fitted with the readiness of the gospel of peace (6:15) and of Christ who came and preached peace to those far off and near (2:17).

Other lines of the chapter reappear too. Paul quotes the Greek of verse 5 in Romans 2:24, but turns it: God's name is blasphemed among the Gentiles not because Israel suffers but because teachers of the law break it. He applies verse 11 to the church's separation from idolatry (2 Corinthians 6:17), and Revelation 18:4 calls God's people to come out of the Babylon of the last days. Verse 10's salvation seen by all the ends of the earth is echoed when Simeon holds the infant Jesus and praises God for the salvation prepared in the sight of all peoples (Luke 2:30-31). Paul quotes verse 15 to explain his aim to preach where Christ was not known (Romans 15:21).

Most striking is the join between verse 12 and verse 13. The announcement that God reigns is followed at once by a Servant who is disfigured and then exalted. The Gospel of John speaks of the Son of Man being ‘lifted up’ and ‘glorified’, the two verbs of the Septuagint of verse 13, and uses them of the cross itself (John 3:14, 12:23, 12:32-34); Peter proclaims that God has glorified his servant Jesus (Acts 3:13); and Paul's hymn in Philippians 2 moves from the one who took the form of a servant to God's exalting him to the highest place. The New Testament reads Jesus' crucifixion and resurrection as the pattern this chapter lays down: the way God's reign actually arrives is through the humiliation and exaltation of his Servant. That reading is a Christian interpretation of the song; Jewish readers have understood the Servant in other ways, as the notes on chapter 53 explain.
interpretation:
Jewish tradition heard the chapter as the promise of final redemption. The Aramaic Targum renders the herald's cry as ‘the kingdom of your God has been revealed’, the same phrase it uses for God's reign elsewhere. At Qumran the Melchizedek scroll (11QMelchizedek, 11Q13) interprets verse 7 of the end time: the messenger is the one anointed by the Spirit, linked with Daniel 9:25 and Isaiah 61, and ‘your God’ who reigns is Melchizedek, who will free God's people from the hand of Belial. The Babylonian Talmud (Sanhedrin 97b) uses verse 3, ‘without money you will be redeemed’, in a debate between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Joshua over whether Israel's redemption depends on repentance; Rabbi Joshua takes the verse to mean that redemption comes by God's will, not as a payment. Pesikta Rabbati 35, a collection of homilies from the early Middle Ages, applies verse 7 to Elijah, who will stand on the mountains of Israel to announce peace before the Messiah comes. The Targum also names the Servant of verse 13 as the Messiah. In the synagogue verses 1 to 12 close the haftarah (the prophetic reading) for the Sabbath of Shoftim, fourth of the seven Sabbaths of consolation that follow the fast of the Ninth of Av; the next week's reading begins at 54:1, so the Servant Song is not read in that cycle. In sixteenth-century Safed Shlomo Alkabetz wove verses 1 and 2, the calls to shake off the dust and put on garments of splendor, into Lekha Dodi, the hymn with which Jewish congregations welcome the Sabbath every Friday evening.

Christian readers took their cue from Paul. Augustine (City of God 18.29) quotes verse 13 in the Greek-based Latin, ‘my servant shall understand, and shall be exalted and glorified exceedingly’, as the Father speaking of Christ, and he says Isaiah prophesied so much of Christ and the church that some would call him an evangelist rather than a prophet. Medieval and Reformation commentators, including Calvin in his commentary on Isaiah, read the herald of verse 7 both of the return from Babylon and of the preaching of the gospel.

Modern critical scholarship reads the chapter within Isaiah 40 to 55, which since Johann Christoph Döderlein and Johann Gottfried Eichhorn in the late eighteenth century most scholars have assigned to a prophet of the exile, and since Bernhard Duhm (1892) it has isolated the Servant Songs as a group. Conservative scholars such as Edward J. Young, John Oswalt (The Book of Isaiah, Chapters 40-66, 1998), and J. Alec Motyer (1993) defend the unity of the book.

In worship, verses 7 to 10 are the Isaiah reading for Christmas Day (Proper III) in the Revised Common Lectionary, and 52:13 to 53:12 is read on Good Friday in all three years. Handel's Messiah (1742) sets the herald's words, in Paul's form from Romans 10:15, as a soprano aria in Part Two. In the early 1970s Leonard E. Smith Jr. built the widely sung chorus Our God Reigns on verse 7.
text:
Several differences between English Bibles come from the Hebrew and the ancient versions. In verse 2 ‘remove the chains’ follows the Masoretic marginal reading (the qere), a command to Zion; the written text (the ketiv) reads ‘the chains of your neck have loosened themselves’. In verse 5 the phrase rendered “those who rule them taunt” is uncertain: the Hebrew may describe Israel's own rulers wailing or the captors howling in triumph, and the ancient versions differ. The Septuagint of verse 5 adds ‘because of you’ and ‘among the Gentiles’ (‘because of you my name is continually blasphemed among the Gentiles’), which is the form Paul quotes in Romans 2:24. The Septuagint of verse 7 is garbled at the start, and Paul's quotation in Romans 10:15 is closer to the Hebrew. The BSB's plural “those who bring good news” generalizes a Hebrew singular, the herald.

In verse 14 the Masoretic Text reads ‘at you’, a sudden address to the Servant, which the Syriac and some Targum manuscripts read as ‘at him’; the BSB follows the latter. The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran (1QIsaa) reads mashachti, ‘I anointed’, where the Masoretic Text has mishchat, ‘disfigurement’; William H. Brownlee argued the scroll's reading was original and messianic, but most scholars keep the Masoretic reading. Verse 15 is the most debated: the KJV, NASB, ESV, and BSB read ‘sprinkle many nations’, taking the verb in its usual priestly sense; the RSV, NRSV, and the Jewish Publication Society's 1985 translation read ‘startle’, from a proposed second root, following the sense of the Septuagint's ‘many nations will marvel at him’. The Septuagint of verse 15 also adds ‘about him’, and Paul quotes that form in Romans 15:21. The Aramaic Targum of verse 13 reads ‘my servant the Messiah’. Chapter and verse numbering is the same in Hebrew and English Bibles.

teach.big: God announces that he reigns and comes home to redeem his people for nothing, calling them to wake, dress for joy, and walk out of captivity under his protection, and he reveals that his victory will be won through a Servant exalted after terrible suffering.

outline.t: God calls his people to believe his rescue before they see it: wake up, dress for the feast, and rise from the dust of captivity.
No one owns God's people but God; sold for nothing, they are redeemed without payment, because he acts for the honor of his name and makes himself known.
The gospel is an announcement, not advice: your God reigns, and the proof is that he has comforted and redeemed his people before the whole world.
Redemption calls for a clean break with the old captivity, and God's people walk out unhurried, with God ahead of them and behind them.
God's reign arrives through his Servant, who will be exalted to the heights after a disfigurement that appalls onlookers, and whose work will reach and silence the nations.

teach.pitfalls:
The most common misuse of this chapter is to lift verse 7 out of its setting and make it a verse about evangelists' feet or about the virtue of sharing good news in general. The herald's message has a specific content, that God reigns and has redeemed Jerusalem, and in the New Testament that content is the kingdom and the cross; the beauty of the feet comes from the news, not the messenger. A second misuse is to separate verses 1 to 12 from verses 13 to 15, as the chapter break before 53:1 tempts readers to do. The song belongs with the herald's message, and preaching the return from exile without the Servant, or the Servant without the good news of God's reign, loses the chapter's point.

A third pitfall is to treat verse 11 as a charter for withdrawal from all contact with outsiders. The command is to leave Babylon's idolatry and uncleanness, and Paul applies it to partnership with idolatry (2 Corinthians 6:14-18), not to avoiding unbelievers, whom he elsewhere tells believers not to shun (1 Corinthians 5:9-10). A fourth is to explain away the historical setting. Whatever one holds about the book's authorship, the chapter speaks to real exiles in Babylon, and its promises were first heard as God's word about their release; the Christian reading builds on that setting rather than replacing it. Finally, be honest that verse 15 has two possible translations and do not build a doctrine on ‘sprinkle’ alone.
teach.pastoral: This chapter speaks to people who feel sold for nothing: those who have been used, trafficked, or treated as worthless, and those who feel their lives were given away by the choices of others. God's words, you were sold for nothing and will be redeemed without money, tell them that no captor has a legitimate claim on them. Teach with care, and do not imply that such people must simply decide to ‘shake off the dust’; the chapter's order is that God redeems and then calls his people to rise. The promise that God is both vanguard and rear guard (verse 12) can comfort those haunted by their past, since God guards the road behind as well as ahead.

hard.q: If Isaiah lived in the eighth century BC, how can this chapter speak so directly to exiles in Babylon two centuries later?
hard.a:
The argument for a later author is the case most critical scholars find decisive. Chapters 40 to 55 assume that Jerusalem has already fallen and its people are in Babylon (compare verse 11 here, “go out from there”), announce that its punishment is over (40:2), and name Cyrus of Persia, who took Babylon in 539 BC, as the LORD's anointed who will let the exiles go (44:28, 45:1). Isaiah of Jerusalem worked in the late eighth century, under Ahaz and Hezekiah. Abraham Ibn Ezra in the twelfth century hinted that these chapters concern the return from Babylon; Johann Christoph Döderlein and Johann Gottfried Eichhorn in the late eighteenth century argued that they came from a prophet of the exile; and Bernhard Duhm's commentary (1892) divided the book into three parts, First, Second, and Third Isaiah. On this view an anonymous prophet in Babylon, writing in the 540s BC, spoke in Isaiah's tradition, and his words were joined to the older prophet's scroll. Skeptical readers add that naming Cyrus more than a century in advance would be a kind of prediction that no historical method can accept.

The traditional view, held by Jewish and Christian readers for most of history and defended by conservative scholars such as Edward J. Young, Oswald T. Allis, John Oswalt, and J. Alec Motyer, is that Isaiah of Jerusalem wrote the whole book and foresaw the exile and the return. Its defenders point to the themes and titles that run through both halves, such as the Holy One of Israel, which occurs about twelve times in chapters 1 to 39 and about fourteen times in chapters 40 to 66, and only about six times in the rest of the Bible; to Isaiah 39:5-7, where Isaiah already foretells the Babylonian captivity; to the argument of chapters 41 to 48 that the LORD proves himself God by announcing events before they happen (41:21-23, 44:7-8, 48:3-5), which assumes real prediction; and to the New Testament, which quotes both halves as the words of Isaiah (John 12:38-41). Many scholars between these positions, including Brevard Childs (Isaiah, 2001), stress that whatever its history of composition, the book was shaped to be read as one, and that its final form presents the whole as Isaiah's vision (1:1). The question of authorship is not a matter of the creeds, and Christians who hold a high view of Scripture answer it in more than one way.

hard.q: The chapter promises that the uncircumcised and unclean will never again enter Jerusalem. Did that promise fail?
hard.a:
The objection is plain. Verse 1 promises that the uncircumcised and unclean will no longer enter Zion, and verses 8 to 10 describe a return seen by all the ends of the earth. Yet the historical return under Cyrus was small and struggling, the city's walls lay in ruins for nearly a century, and Jerusalem was entered and defiled again and again: by the Seleucid king Antiochus IV, who set up a pagan altar in the temple in 167 BC (1 Maccabees 1:54), by Pompey in 63 BC, and by the Romans, who destroyed the temple in AD 70. Robert Carroll (When Prophecy Failed, 1979) applied the psychology of cognitive dissonance to the prophets, arguing that prophetic traditions grew by reinterpreting expectations that history did not meet, and skeptical readers see this chapter as a clear example.

Those who read the promise as God's word respond in several ways. Many Jewish interpreters, ancient and modern, read the chapter as a promise of final redemption still awaited, which is why the rabbis applied it to the Messiah's coming (Pesikta Rabbati 35) and why the synagogue reads it in the season of consolation after mourning the temple's fall. Christian interpreters often read it in stages: a first fulfillment in the return from Babylon, a deeper one in the coming of the Servant, and a final one in the new Jerusalem, of which Revelation says “nothing unclean will ever enter it” (Revelation 21:27). N. T. Wright (The New Testament and the People of God, 1992) argued that many Jews of the first century believed the exile had not truly ended because these promises remained unfulfilled, and that the early Christians understood Jesus' death and resurrection as the real end of exile. Commentators such as John Oswalt read the passage's language as deliberately larger than any single historical return. How literally to expect a future restoration of Jerusalem is a question on which Christians differ, but both Jewish and Christian readers have agreed that the chapter's horizon reaches past 538 BC.

observe: What three commands does God give Zion in verses 1 and 2, and what is she told to leave behind?
What four things does the messenger proclaim in verse 7, and what do the watchmen see in verse 8?
How does the departure of verse 12 differ from Israel's departure from Egypt, and who goes before and behind the people?
interpret: What does it mean that Israel was ‘sold for nothing’ and will be redeemed ‘without money’ (verse 3)? What claim does that remove from Babylon?
Why is God's name blasphemed when his people are defeated (verse 5), and how does their rescue answer that dishonor?
Why do you think the announcement ‘Your God reigns’ is followed immediately by the portrait of a disfigured and exalted Servant (verses 13 to 15)?
apply: The herald brings news, not advice. How would your sharing of the gospel change if you thought of it as announcing something God has done?
What ‘Babylon’ are you still carrying with you that God calls you to leave behind, and what would it look like to walk out unhurried with him as your rear guard?
Where in your community could you be like the watchmen, the first to see and shout that God has comforted his people?
